summary: Defines the Mobile-IPv4 Configuration Option for IPCP. It lets two peers on a PPP link say they support Mobile IP, so foreign agents need not give each mobile node a unique address.

eli5.summary: This lets a traveling device tell the network it is a mobile one while connecting, so it can keep its home address wherever it goes.

questions: what is the mobile-ipv4 ipcp option
how does mobile ip work over ppp
subtitle: A PPP option that lets a mobile device say it speaks Mobile IP, so it need not be handed a unique address.

tldr.problem: Mobile IP says little about PPP. A mobile node that proposes its home address in IPCP gets a conservative Configure-Nak, so it ends up with a unique assigned address even when the peer is a foreign agent.
tldr.mechanism: The Mobile-IPv4 Configuration Option (type 4, length 6) carries the mobile node's home address. Used together with the IP-Address option, it lets both ends negotiate whether the node is at home, uses a co-located care-of address, or uses the peer as a foreign agent.
tldr.outcome: Foreign agents can serve PPP mobile nodes without assigning each a unique address. The RFC updates RFC 2002 and is itself updated by RFC 2794.

today: RFC 2290 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2002 and is itself updated by RFC 2794. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Mobile IP (RFC 2002) lets packets reach a mobile node wherever it attaches to the Internet, without changing its IP address. It is designed to run over any link layer. But its interaction with PPP is underspecified and generally leads to Mobile IP being applied inappropriately when mobile nodes connect via PPP.

This RFC defines a new option for the Internet Protocol Control Protocol (IPCP, RFC 1332), the Mobile-IPv4 Configuration Option. The mobile node and its PPP peer use it to negotiate the proper use of Mobile IP on the link. It works together with the existing IP-Address option. The document assumes familiarity with Mobile IP, IPCP and PPP (RFC 1661).
sections.eli5: Mobile IP lets a gadget keep one permanent address while it moves around. This note teaches it how to say so when it plugs in with a phone-line style connection.

sections.title: The Problem with IPCP Today
sections.content:
In Mobile IP, packets for a mobile node's home address go first to its home agent, which tunnels them to a care-of address. A co-located care-of address is assigned to the mobile node itself and can be used by only one node at a time. A foreign agent care-of address belongs to a foreign agent and can be shared by many mobile nodes at once.

The existing text in RFC 2002 Appendix B says the node should first try to specify its home address in IPCP. Walking through that negotiation shows the flaw. The mobile node proposes its home address in an IP-Address option. The peer cannot tell whether that is a mobile node or an ordinary node with a non-routable address, so it conservatively sends a Configure-Nak with a topologically appropriate address. The mobile node in turn cannot tell whether the peer is a cautious foreign agent or has no Mobile IP at all, so it keeps negotiating and ends up using the assigned address as a co-located care-of address.

That defeats the point of foreign agent care-of addresses, which exist so that many mobile nodes can share one address and none needs a unique one.
sections.eli5: The device asks for its own home address, and the other side cannot tell if it is a traveler or just confused. So it hands out a brand new address, which wastes the sharing trick.

sections.title: Design Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC states four requirements for the option and protocol:

  • It must be backwards compatible with conventional nodes and peers that implement neither this option nor any Mobile IP.
  • It must handle a variety of scenarios, at least those in the examples of Section 2.6.
  • It must not duplicate functionality already in other IPCP options, specifically the IP-Address option.
  • A unique address must not be assigned to a mobile node unless absolutely necessary. None is assigned to a node on its home link or one that uses a foreign agent's care-of address.
sections.eli5: The rules are: do not break old devices, do not copy what existing options do, and only hand out a private address if there is no other way.

sections.title: The Mobile-IPv4 Configuration Option
sections.content:
The option has three fields: Type is 4 (Mobile-IPv4), Length is 6 (the length of the entire option in bytes) and the last field is the mobile node's home address.

In a Configure-Request the address is the home address of the sender. In a Configure-Ack or Configure-Reject it is the unmodified home address from the request. The field MUST NOT be zero. Configure-Nak of this option is undefined and MUST NOT be sent. The default value is the sending mobile node's home address.

A node that is not acting as a mobile node, including nodes that only perform home agent or foreign agent functions, MUST NOT put this option in a Configure-Request. A peer that is neither home agent nor foreign agent SHOULD Reject any request that contains it. A node that sends a Configure-Ack with the option SHOULD send an Agent Advertisement as soon as IPCP reaches the Opened state.
sections.eli5: The option is a short label that says "I am a traveler" and includes the traveler's permanent address. Helpers who are not travelers should never use it.

sections.title: How the Negotiation Works
sections.content:
Section 2.5 lists every combination of the Mobile-IPv4 option and the IP-Address option a node might send, with the responses a peer MUST choose from. A mobile node SHOULD begin with item 1, Request(IP=0,MIPv4=home), meaning it prefers a co-located care-of address, or item 4, Request(MIPv4=home), meaning it wants Mobile IP without a co-located address and will use a foreign agent care-of address.

Typical answers to item 1 are a Nak giving a care-of address, a Nak with the home address (meaning the node is at home), or Reject of the IP-Address option (meaning the peer cannot assign an address but can act as a foreign agent). If the peer rejects the Mobile-IPv4 option instead, it does not implement it, and the node falls back to ordinary IP-Address negotiation.

A mobile node that gets a Configure-Ack with the option MUST wait for an Agent Advertisement before sending a Registration Request when on a foreign link, since the peer may require registration even for a co-located address. It need not wait at its home link. If the option is rejected, the node SHOULD fall back to the IP-Address option, starting with Request(IP=home) on its home link or Request(IP=0) otherwise. This updates RFC 2002, which recommends starting with the home address in all circumstances.
sections.eli5: The traveler opens with its preferred question, and the other side answers yes, no, or here is a different address. If the other side does not understand, the traveler just asks the old way.

sections.title: Example Scenarios
sections.content:
Section 2.6 walks through six scenarios (A to F). In scenario A the peer is a foreign agent that can assign an address: the node sends Request(IP=0,MIPv4=Home), gets Nak(IP=coa), then asks for that address and receives an Ack. It then waits for an Agent Advertisement before registering.

In scenario B the peer cannot assign an address, so it Rejects the IP-Address option. The node then sends Request(MIPv4=Home), gets an Ack, and registers using the peer's foreign agent care-of address. In scenario C the peer replies with a Nak carrying the home address, so the node learns it is at home and de-registers with its home agent.

Scenarios E and F cover peers without the option. In E the peer can still assign dynamic addresses, and the node uses the assigned address as a co-located care-of address. In F the peer cannot, so the node sends an Agent Solicitation, tries other means such as DHCP or manual configuration, or gives up.
sections.eli5: The RFC shows six little stories: at home, visiting a helpful host, visiting a host that cannot give an address, and visiting an old host that does not know the trick.

sections.title: Other Options and Move Detection
sections.content:
A mobile node MUST NOT include the deprecated IP-Addresses option in a Configure-Request that has a Mobile-IPv4 option, an IP-Address option, or both. It MAY include IP-Compression-Protocol and other options that do not negotiate addresses. If PPP peers agree on Van Jacobson header compression (RFC 1144), the node MUST NOT set the V bit in its Mobile IP Registration Request.

Because movement will likely change the PPP peer, mobile nodes MUST be ready to renegotiate IPCP at any time, including both options. A node in the Opened state MUST renegotiate upon receiving an IPCP Configure-Request from its peer. Some wireless links hand off without bringing PPP down, so nodes MUST still run their Mobile IP move detection and register whenever connectivity changes. A node that stops receiving Agent Advertisements within the advertised Lifetime MUST assume it lost contact with that foreign agent.
sections.eli5: A traveler must always be ready to redo its introduction, because when it moves, the helper on the other end may change.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it introduces no known security threats beyond those facing any node that connects via PPP or implements Mobile IP. Service providers should use cryptographically strong authentication, for example CHAP (RFC 1994), to prevent theft of service. Users who need confidentiality should use PPP link encryption (RFC 1968), IP-layer encryption (RFC 1827) or application-layer encryption. Mobile IP authentication protects against trivial denial-of-service attacks on a mobile node and its home agent.
sections.eli5: The new label adds no new dangers. The usual locks, like passwords and scrambling, are still the way to stay safe.
